newsitem.title: BELGIUM: NATO agrees to new 18-month mission in Bosnia.
newsitem.headline: NATO agrees to new 18-month mission in Bosnia.

text.p: NATO agreed on Wednesday that its new Stabilisation Force (SFOR) in Bosnia should stay in the country for no more than 18 months, with reviews every six months to decide needed troop levels.

Ambassadors from the 16-nation alliance agreed to a timetable outlined two weeks ago by U.S. President Bill Clinton for a follow-on force to replace the NATO-led Implementation Force (IFOR) when its mandate expires on December 20.

"This sets the alliance fair for the future...and reflects a recognition that we can continue to play a constructive role," Robert Hunter, U.S. ambassador to the North Atlantic Treaty Organisation, told Reuters.
NATO last week agreed in principle to plan for about 30,000 international troops to stay on in Bosnia next year. But the issue of how long the new SFOR mission would stay was left undecided.
The alliance had been thinking in terms of one year, with France saying that two years may be needed.
Clinton surprised America's allies on November 16 by saying that Washington would keep its troops in Bosnia for 18 months, reviewing their presence every six months.

"There was a certain amount of consternation because everyone had been assuming a force for one year and the Americans...without any prior consultation, announced 18 months," Emyr Jones Parry, deputy political director at Britain's Foreign Office, said on Tuesday.
"There then followed an accelerated consideration in Brussels of what the Americans had proposed and how it should be taken forward," he told a parliamentary committee in London.
Hunter admitted that the U.S. move had caught Washington's allies unprepared, but said they were glad of America's commitment.
"The allies were surprised initially that the United States was prepared to go as far as we were," he said. "They had hoped we would be willing to go for a year."
NATO has insisted all along that the alliance is not willing to have an open-ended mission in Bosnia.
"No one wants to stay longer than necessary," Hunter said, underlining that the U.S. troops would be gone by mid-1998.
IFOR, which at its height had about 60,000 troops, was given a one-year mandate, which is effectively now being extended by the new, leaner force.
Alliance officials have in the past emphasised the need for deadlines, citing the 32 years of United Nations presence in Cyprus as an example of what it wants to avoid.
The ambassadors also agreed a mandate for the new SFOR. It will be available for help with next year's muncipal elections and for some work on Bosnian reconstruction.
"Clearly (with fewer troops) it will have to be more selective," a NATO source said.

But there was no question of the NATO-led force acting as Bosnia's policeman. "We cannot and will not do police work. No police work," the source said, adding that this extended, as it does now, to not hunting down alleged war criminals.
